In [Calls and Patient Journeys](04_calls_and_patient_journeys.qmd) we saw `DES_HEMS` turn each daily call into a `Patient` and ask for a resource, and we saw it trigger a "daily servicing check" at the start of every simulated day. This chapter looks at the other side of that request: what a resource *is*, where the list of resources comes from, and how the model keeps unavailable ones out of reach.

## The use case: a helicopter that is due a service {#sec-hems-resources-and-servicing-use-case}

Devon Air Ambulance operates two helicopters (registrations `g-daas` and `g-daan`) and three rapid-response cars. A helicopter cannot fly while it is being serviced, and a service takes about three weeks. If the simulation ignored this, a scenario with fewer aircraft would look better than it deserves.

So the model has to answer three questions before a single patient is created:

1. Which resources exist, and when are they on shift?
2. When will each one be in for servicing, over the whole simulated period?
3. On any given day, which resources can be handed to a patient, and which are parked in the workshop?

We will follow one helicopter, `g-daas`, through all three. The answers live in three small classes (`Ambulance`, `HEMS` and `HEMSAvailability`) and several CSV files in `actual_data/`, the folder that the app fills in ([Streamlit App and Scenario Parameters](01_streamlit_app_and_scenario_parameters.qmd)).

::: {.column-margin}
**HEMS resource**: one helicopter or car, as an instance of `HEMS`. A single physical vehicle can appear as more than one HEMS resource (see below).
:::

## Key concepts {#sec-hems-resources-and-servicing-concepts}

### Ambulance and HEMS

[Ambulance](../reference/class_ambulance.Ambulance.qmd) is the generic "something that responds to an incident". It holds a type, a callsign and a handful of timestamp placeholders for the stages of a job.

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_ambulance.py" start-line=16 end-line=28 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_ambulance.py:16-28" include-hash="aa7ecca71219"}
```

It is deliberately thin. All the interesting behaviour lives in its subclass [HEMS](../reference/class_hems.HEMS.qmd), which adds the attributes the allocation logic needs:

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems.py" start-line=15 end-line=69 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems.py:15-69" code-line-style="dim:34-49" include-hash="d7c1a3ed6526"}
```

The attributes worth knowing:

callsign and callsign group
:   The callsign (for example `H70` or `CC72`) is what the crew is called on the radio. The callsign group (an integer such as `70`) ties together the vehicles that share one crew: the helicopter `H70` and the car `CC70` are staffed by the same people, so they must never be out at the same time. The allocation code in [Resource Allocation](06_resource_allocation.qmd) relies on this.

registration
:   The identifier of the physical vehicle (`g-daas`, `cc70`). Servicing is a property of the registration, not the callsign.

vehicle type and category
:   `helicopter` or `car`, and a care category (`CC` critical care or `EC` enhanced care) describing the clinical capability the resource is being used for. Care categories were introduced in [Calls and Patient Journeys](04_calls_and_patient_journeys.qmd).

summer and winter shift hours
:   Four hour-of-day values giving when the resource starts and stops work in each season. The months that count as summer are read from `actual_data/rota_start_end_months.csv` (the dimmed method in the excerpt above).

servicing schedule
:   A small DataFrame of `service_start_date` and `service_end_date` rows, calculated up front and handed to the resource when it is built.

`in_use` and `being_serviced`
:   Two flags that the allocation code reads. `in_use` is set while a patient has the resource; `being_serviced` is updated whenever the servicing schedule is checked.

### Shifts: `hems_resource_on_shift`

The shift check is a pure function of the hour and the month.

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems.py" start-line=107 end-line=120 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems.py:107-120" code-line-style="hi:11-14" include-hash="796c15ba7507"}
```

[`hems_resource_on_shift`](../reference/class_hems.HEMS.qmd) picks the summer or winter hours depending on the month (highlighted), then asks `Utils.is_time_in_range` whether the hour falls inside them. That helper copes with shifts that cross midnight: in `utils.py` it returns `start <= current < end` when `start <= end`, and `current >= start or current < end` otherwise. This matters because the `H70` enhanced-care row in the rota runs from 19 to 2.

### The rota: one row per role, not per vehicle

`actual_data/HEMS_ROTA.csv` has one row per callsign *and* care category:

```{.text .illustrative filename="Example: actual_data/HEMS_ROTA.csv (first rows)"}
callsign,category,vehicle_type,callsign_group,summer_start,winter_start,summer_end,winter_end
H70,CC,helicopter,70,7,7,19,19
H70,EC,helicopter,70,19,19,2,2
CC70,CC,car,70,7,7,19,19
CC70,EC,car,70,19,19,2,2
```

The shipped file also has rows for `H71` (an enhanced care helicopter) and `CC72` (an enhanced care car). The same aircraft therefore appears twice: as a critical-care helicopter by day and as an enhanced-care helicopter overnight. Each row becomes its own `HEMS` object, and both objects share the registration `g-daas`. That is why you will see the code identify a resource by *category and registration together*, and why the active registrations tracked during allocation matter: they stop the same airframe being sent in both roles at once.

## Building the resources {#sec-hems-resources-and-servicing-building}

[HEMSAvailability](../reference/class_hems_availability.HEMSAvailability.qmd) is the class that owns all of this. It is created once per run by `DES_HEMS` and is where the two SimPy stores live.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Refresher: SimPy FilterStore"}
A SimPy `Store` is a queue of Python objects: `put(item)` adds one and `get()` removes one, waiting (in simulated time) if none is available. A `FilterStore` adds a `get(filter)` variant that takes the first item for which the filter function returns true. Both `put` and `get` return events, so inside a process you write `item = yield store.get(...)`.
:::

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py" start-line=99 end-line=123 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py:99-123" code-line-style="hi:9-12,dim:1-8" include-hash="4c026167d1c1"}
```

Two stores are created. `store` holds resources that are in the base and may be dispatched. `serviceStore` is the **service store**: a holding area for anything currently in the workshop. Moving a resource between them is how the model takes it out of circulation, with no extra "is it serviced?" test needed on the hot path of allocation (though `being_serviced` is still checked, as a second line of defence).

The constructor then calls `prep_HEMS_resources()` to build the objects and `populate_store()` to put them in `store`. Finally it runs a daily servicing check, in case the simulation starts mid-service (see the warning below).

### Reading the rota and servicing files

[`prep_HEMS_resources`](../reference/class_hems_availability.HEMSAvailability.qmd) starts by joining three small tables:

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py" start-line=229 end-line=241 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py:229-241" include-hash="e9e3420aa51f"}
```

- `service_schedules_by_model.csv` says how often each aircraft *model* is serviced (`service_schedule_months`) and for how many weeks (`service_duration_weeks`).
- `callsign_registration_lookup.csv` maps each registration to a callsign and a model.
- `service_history.csv` gives the date each registration was last serviced. Cars have a `0` there, which `na_values=0` turns into a missing value, so they never get a service schedule.

The result is one row per registration with everything needed to project its future services.

### Projecting service dates

For each registration with a known last service, the method walks forward in time until it passes the simulation end date, asking `find_next_service_date` for each next slot.

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py" start-line=245 end-line=288 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py:245-288" code-line-style="hi:17-22" include-hash="10cf025c3578"}
```

The highlighted call is the heart of it. Each result is appended three ways: to `schedule` (every registration, which becomes the DataFrame written to `data/service_dates.csv`), to `service_dates` (a list shared across *all* resources, so later aircraft can avoid earlier ones), and to `current_resource_service_dates`. The `end_date` computed just before the call (which uses the servicing buffer) is overwritten by the call's return value.

The loop's bound is `self.sim_end_date`, which the constructor sets to the simulation end plus an extra 365 days. The comment there explains why: a service date can be walked backwards into the previous year, so the schedule needs some slack.

### Choosing a date: `find_next_service_date`

[`find_next_service_date`](../reference/class_hems_availability.HEMSAvailability.qmd) starts from "last service plus the interval", then prefers a configured month if that is possible, then nudges earlier until the slot is legal.

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py" start-line=749 end-line=779 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py:749-779" code-line-style="hi:14-31" include-hash="923f912c3db3"}
```

The preferred date is the 2nd of `servicing_preferred_month` (January by default) in the year the service falls due. If the service is due after that month, the preferred date rolls to the next year. The preferred date is only used if it is on or before the due date and does not clash with school holidays; it is never later than the due date, so an aircraft is never serviced late.

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py" start-line=781 end-line=793 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py:781-793" include-hash="288a93ffd08b"}
```

The loop is simple and a little brutal: while the proposed window overlaps a school holiday ([`is_during_school_holidays`](../reference/class_hems_availability.HEMSAvailability.qmd)) or another resource's service ([`is_other_resource_being_serviced`](../reference/class_hems_availability.HEMSAvailability.qmd)), move the start one day earlier and try again. Both helpers rely on [`do_ranges_overlap`](../reference/class_hems_availability.HEMSAvailability.qmd), which is the standard interval test `max(start1, start2) <= min(end1, end2)`.

::: {.callout-tip}
**School holidays** are loaded in the constructor with `load_school_holidays("actual_data/school_holidays.csv")` from `school_holidays.py`. The function accepts UK dates (`dd/mm/yyyy`, as in the shipped CSV) or ISO dates (as written by the app when you import a template), trying UK format first, and raises a `ValueError` if a holiday ends before it starts. Servicing is steered away from these periods by the search loop above.
:::

### Turning rows into `HEMS` objects

With the service dates in a DataFrame, the rota is read and merged with the servicing information, and each row becomes a resource:

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py" start-line=299 end-line=325 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py:299-325" code-line-style="hi:4" include-hash="9f84b7239d62"}
```

The merge on `callsign` and `vehicle_type` is what attaches a registration and a model to each rota row. Each resource gets only its own registration's slice of the servicing table (`s`). Finally `populate_store` simply calls `self.store.put(h)` for every object in `HEMS_resources_list`.

@fig-hems-resources-and-servicing-build summarises the flow from CSV files to stores.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-hems-resources-and-servicing-build
%%| fig-cap: "From input files to the two stores"
flowchart LR
    A[HEMS_ROTA.csv] --> P[prep_HEMS_resources]
    B[callsign_registration_lookup.csv] --> P
    C[service_schedules_by_model.csv] --> P
    D[service_history.csv] --> P
    E[school_holidays.csv] --> F[find_next_service_date]
    P --> F
    F --> P
    P --> L[HEMS objects with servicing schedules]
    L --> S[(store)]
    S <-->|daily_servicing_check| W[(serviceStore)]
```

## The daily servicing check {#sec-hems-resources-and-servicing-daily-check}

Schedules are fixed up front, but the stores only change when the check runs. `DES_HEMS.generate_calls` runs it once at the start of every simulated day:

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/des_hems.py" start-line=245 end-line=248 filename="air_ambulance_des/des_hems.py:245-248" include-hash="63f4821e25c1"}
```

Because `daily_servicing_check` is a generator containing `yield` statements, it must be wrapped in `env.process` and yielded, which blocks the call generator until the shuffling is done. @fig-hems-resources-and-servicing-check shows what happens inside.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-hems-resources-and-servicing-check
%%| fig-cap: "One daily servicing check, simplified"
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as DES_HEMS
    participant A as HEMSAvailability
    participant H as HEMS (g-daas)
    participant S as serviceStore
    participant M as store
    D->>A: daily_servicing_check(current_dt)
    A->>H: unavailable_due_to_service(current_dt)
    H-->>A: True or False (GDAAS_service)
    loop each resource in serviceStore
        A->>H: service_check(current_dt, GDAAS_service)
        H-->>A: still in service?
        A->>S: get finished resource
        A->>M: put it back
    end
    loop each resource in store
        A->>H: service_check(current_dt, GDAAS_service)
        H-->>A: due for service?
        A->>M: get resource
        A->>S: put it in the workshop
    end
```

The first half of the method decides who is coming back:

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py" start-line=139 end-line=173 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py:139-173" code-line-style="hi:3-7,hi:12-16" include-hash="d2b3e22475eb"}
```

It first looks for the resource registered as `g-daas` and asks whether it is in service today, storing the answer as `GDAAS_service`. Then it builds a list of `(category, registration)` pairs from `serviceStore` whose `service_check` is now false (note the `not`). It collects the pairs first and moves them afterwards, because changing a store while iterating over its `items` would be unsafe. Each move is a `get` with a filter on category and registration, followed by a `put` on the main store. Filtering on both is necessary because of the two-objects-per-airframe point made earlier.

The second half is the mirror image:

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py" start-line=175 end-line=198 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems_availability.py:175-198" include-hash="4290373776ce"}
```

Anything in `store` for which `service_check` returns true is taken out and placed in `serviceStore`. Further down, the method only logs status through [`current_store_status`](../reference/class_hems_availability.HEMSAvailability.qmd), which is a debugging helper.

### The shared aircraft: H70 and H71

Devon has two helicopters, but the rota only knows two callsigns, H70 and H71. When the usual H70 aircraft (`g-daas`) is in the workshop, the other aircraft must fly as H70 so that the callsign-group-70 crew can still be dispatched. `service_check` (the second method in the `HEMS` excerpt above) implements that by rewriting the callsign and group on the `g-daan` resource:

| Aircraft | `g-daas` in service | `g-daas` not in service |
|---|---|---|
| `g-daas` | in the workshop | `H70` |
| `g-daan` | `H70` (callsign group 70) | `H71` |

The code is at `class_hems.py:71-89`:

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems.py" start-line=71 end-line=89 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems.py:71-89" code-line-style="hi:2-13" include-hash="ca437507dfcd"}
```

When `g-daas` is in for servicing (`GDAAS_service` true), `g-daan` takes over as `H70`; when `g-daas` returns, it reverts to `H71`. Either way, the method ends by returning [`unavailable_due_to_service`](../reference/class_hems.HEMS.qmd), which scans the resource's own service windows:

```{.python include="../../air_ambulance_des/class_hems.py" start-line=91 end-line=105 filename="air_ambulance_des/class_hems.py:91-105" code-line-style="hi:8-12" include-hash="e929656f0f91"}
```

That is the only place `being_serviced` is set: it is true if `current_dt` lies inside any `[service_start_date, service_end_date]` window. Because it is a linear scan of a short table once a day per resource, its cost is negligible.

`current_dt` itself comes from `Utils.date_time_of_call`, which converts simulation minutes into a calendar date; see [Sampling Distributions and Random Streams](03_sampling_distributions_and_random_streams.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning title="A call that does nothing in the constructor"}
`HEMSAvailability.__init__` ends with `self.daily_servicing_check(current_dt, hod, month)`, with the comment "in case sim starts during a service". But `daily_servicing_check` is a generator function, and calling a generator function without iterating it (or wrapping it in `env.process`) runs none of its body. As written, that constructor call appears to be a no-op. In practice the first real check happens when `generate_calls` starts day one, at simulation time zero, so the effect is limited to anything that happens before that point. It is worth knowing if you ever construct `HEMSAvailability` outside `DES_HEMS` and expect the stores to be correct immediately.
:::

## Tracing `g-daas` through a run {#sec-hems-resources-and-servicing-trace}

Putting it together for our helicopter:

1. **Setup.** `prep_HEMS_resources` reads its last service date from `service_history.csv` (4 January 2022) and its model's interval (8 months for the Airbus H145, 3 weeks duration, as the shipped CSVs stand). It projects service windows until a year past the simulation end, avoiding school holidays and the other aircraft's windows. Two `HEMS` objects (CC and EC) are created with these windows and put in `store`.
2. **Every morning.** The check runs. Most days nothing moves.
3. **Service starts.** `unavailable_due_to_service` becomes true for `g-daas`. Both of its `HEMS` objects move to `serviceStore`, and `g-daan` takes the `H70` callsign for the duration.
4. **During the service.** [Resource Allocation](06_resource_allocation.qmd) iterates over `store.items`, so the grounded aircraft cannot be seen, let alone chosen.
5. **Service ends.** The next morning's check sees the window has passed, moves both objects back and `g-daan` reverts to `H71`.

The shipped `service_schedules_by_model.csv` gives the H145 an 8-month interval and the EC135 a 12-month interval, with a 3-week duration for each; cars have `0` and never enter the workshop. The preferred month is a constructor argument of `HEMSAvailability`. A `servicing_buffer_weeks` argument (default 4) also exists, but the buffer is only used in a value that is overwritten straight away, so it does not currently lengthen the service windows (a service window is exactly the model's `service_duration_weeks`).

## Conclusion {#sec-hems-resources-and-servicing-conclusion}

A resource is a `HEMS` object (a subclass of `Ambulance`) with a callsign, callsign group, registration, vehicle type, care category, seasonal shift hours and a pre-computed servicing schedule. `HEMSAvailability` builds them from the rota and servicing CSVs, plans service windows that dodge school holidays and each other, keeps dispatchable resources in a `FilterStore`, and parks serviced ones in a second store through a daily check.

Next, in [Resource Allocation](06_resource_allocation.qmd), we will see how `HEMSAvailability` searches that store for the best resource for each patient, records the reason for its choice and releases the resource afterwards.
